samples.subject: Math
samples.stuck: freezes before trying; writes column totals side by side instead of carrying
samples.loves: building marble runs and LEGO
samples.approach: models carrying as marbles overflowing from the ones track into the tens track

samples.subject: Reading
samples.stuck: says each letter sound correctly but cannot push the sounds together into a word
samples.loves: dinosaurs
samples.approach: every blending exercise uses chunks from dinosaur names, starting with short names and building to five-chunk names like Velociraptor

samples.subject: Science
samples.stuck: keeping mixed ages engaged together without the oldest waiting and the youngest drifting
samples.loves: bugs, the backyard, splashing water
samples.approach: the oldest reads and teaches; the youngest two do and touch; short bursts with a hands-on reset between each part

samples.subject: Math
samples.stuck: the younger thinks a bigger bottom number means a bigger piece; the older can name fractions but not add halves and quarters
samples.loves: baking at the kitchen table together
samples.approach: one baking activity, two levels: the little one halves and quarters real dough; the older adds the fractions that make up the recipe

samples.subject: Writing
samples.stuck: can argue a point out loud for ten minutes but freezes when asked to put the same case in a written paragraph
samples.loves: hockey — playing it, watching it, arguing about it
samples.approach: picks up from session one's next-time note: turn a spoken hockey argument into a paragraph with a claim, two reasons, and a line that answers the other side

samples.subject: Math
samples.stuck: reads the hour hand but not the minutes; cannot yet work out how long until something happens
samples.loves: buses, and the real timetable at the stop near home
samples.approach: a real bus timetable on one folded printed page, one question at a time, with the guide's answer key kept separate

samples.subject: Science
samples.stuck: can recite the words evaporation and condensation but cannot say what is actually happening to the water or why
samples.loves: watching things change — melting, freezing, anything that transforms in front of him
samples.approach: builds the whole cycle in a sealed jar on a sunny sill so the learner watches evaporation and condensation happen, then names each step from what he saw

samples.subject: History
samples.stuck: treats history as dates and names to memorise and cannot see it as something that happened to actual people
samples.loves: the family's own stories, and talking with older relatives who remember things
samples.approach: turns one session into a real interview with a grandparent about a small town — what it looked like, one job they held, one change they lived through — then shapes the answers into the start of a local history

samples.subject: Math
samples.stuck: no prior fractions; curious about the why but cannot yet say what a fraction means or how a shape can be divided into equal parts
samples.loves: football and running
samples.approach: seven steps in a 3D stadium in French — the pitch halved into equal parts, runners on the 400 m track compared, laps added and subtracted, balls shared into hoops, the whole found back, and a ten-penalty final

samples.subject: Math
samples.stuck: can count on to reach a fact but has not made the facts automatic; rebuilds every answer from one
samples.loves: dominoes — matching the tiles, standing them up, toppling the runs
samples.approach: strategy-first facts (doubles, doubles plus one, make ten) read off domino tiles, five minutes a day, stepping up after a streak

samples.subject: Reading
samples.stuck: reads every word aloud accurately but cannot say what a passage was about afterwards
samples.loves: animals and surprising true facts about them
samples.approach: question first, one short chunk, say it back in one sentence, point to the sentence that proves it — built on short animal-fact passages

samples.subject: Other
samples.stuck: arrived home learning behind in both reading and maths, with scattered gaps, and the guide cannot tell where to restart
samples.loves: crossing the creek on stepping stones and finding the safe way across
samples.approach: a short, kind check that walks back through the early reading and maths stones — letter sounds, blending, adding within ten, tens and ones — to the earliest wobble, and starts there

samples.subject: Writing
samples.stuck: reads a little but writes a string of random letters for a spelling word, because he does not yet hear the separate sounds in it
samples.loves: lining up and sorting small things — buttons, bottle tops, counters
samples.approach: say a short word, push one counter for each sound heard, then write one letter per counter — CVC words first, then digraphs as a single counter

samples.subject: Reading
samples.stuck: after a read-aloud or short passage, cannot recall it, or gives a one-sentence summary that misses the point
samples.loves: drawing, and telling the story in a picture before saying it in words
samples.approach: shorter chunks first, then three fingers — who, what happened, how it ended — said in a row as the summary; a quick three-box sketch for picture-thinkers

samples.subject: Writing
samples.stuck: capable and careful, but freezes and writes nothing when asked to write something open-ended
samples.loves: getting things exactly right, and building from clear step-by-step instructions
samples.approach: remove the choices — a topic-sentence frame with three because-slots filled aloud first, then rewrite a model paragraph with one change and grow from there

samples.subject: Math
samples.stuck: gets upset and walks away whenever he gets something wrong — a count, a puzzle piece, a letter — so being wrong ends the work before it starts
samples.loves: catching a grown-up out, and being the one who knows better
samples.approach: do it together first, then the guide makes deliberate mistakes for the child to catch, so being wrong becomes funny and safe; five to ten minutes, stop while he is winning

samples.subject: Writing
samples.stuck: traces letters and short sentences neatly, and the parent wonders whether tracing is enough writing or whether something more should be happening
samples.loves: telling you about her day, and drawing pictures of what she did
samples.approach: the child says one sentence about her day and the guide writes it down for her to copy a word or two of; the child labels her own drawings by writing the sounds she hears

samples.subject: Reading
samples.stuck: reads decodable readers fine in lessons but will not try a real book on his own — closes it, or asks to be read to instead
samples.loves: being read to, and animals; reading a page out loud to the cat
samples.approach: take turns reading, the guide a page and the child a line, growing the child's share slowly; real books a notch easier than lesson level; read to a pet to take the pressure off

samples.subject: Math
samples.stuck: counts out loud to ten by rote but cannot say how many are in a small pile — the words are a song, not yet a count of things
samples.loves: lining up the small things she already plays with — toy cars, pasta shapes, blocks
samples.approach: count real things she lines up: touch and move one at a time, answer 'how many?' with the last number said, then 'one more', then subitise small groups on a plate — no worksheets

samples.subject: Science
samples.stuck: treats science as facts to be told and has stopped wondering out loud — never asks why things happen, and waits to be given the answer
samples.loves: noticing odd little things around the house and garden, and being proved right
samples.approach: a family habit: one question on the fridge on Monday, a written guess, one small at-home test or look-up midweek, a two-sentence answer on Friday in the learner's own words — the guide asks, never lectures

samples.subject: Science
samples.stuck: learns a science word for the quiz and loses it a week later — the definition was memorised, never attached to anything real
samples.loves: making things, drawing, and doing rather than being told
samples.approach: each word gets an object or action, the learner's own definition, a drawing, and a sentence about something he actually did that week; a running word wall reviewed two minutes a day; at most three new words a week

samples.subject: Writing
samples.stuck: can do a grammar worksheet but cannot find the same thing in a real sentence, or use it in his own writing — the rule and the reading live in separate boxes
samples.loves: the adventure book he is reading at bedtime, and being the expert on its story
samples.approach: grammar from tonight's chapter: pick three sentences from the book he is already reading; one move per session — find the doer and the doing, join two short sentences, change the time of a sentence — his own sentence last; no workbook

samples.subject: Reading
samples.stuck: the parent works from home and cannot see how lessons fit a working day, and the learner drifts when a lesson runs long
samples.loves: trains, and knowing the order things come in — lining the day up like cars on a track
samples.approach: about ninety minutes of guided work in short, predictable blocks around the parent's calls — reading about twenty minutes, maths about fifteen, writing about ten, in two or three sittings — with one visible picture schedule the learner ticks, and the rest of the day play, chores, outside time and a read-aloud; stop on a win

samples.subject: Math
samples.stuck: multi-digit multiplication and long division keep falling apart, and the parent is about to switch maths programmes to fix it
samples.loves: the coin jar — sorting it, and trading ten pennies for a dime
samples.approach: before switching anything, a five-minute check to find the one topic: which times-table facts are automatic and which are counted out, then place value with base-ten blocks or coins, then a single two-digit-by-one-digit problem talked through — fix the earliest wobble first with five minutes a day of facts, and only then judge the programme

samples.subject: Reading
samples.stuck: programme's seated lessons have stopped being fun for either of them; the learner will not sit through them
samples.loves: running, jumping, being on the move all day
samples.approach: keep the programme; move it off the table — letters chalked on the path to hop to, magnetic letters built standing at the fridge, writing big on the wall or with chalk; five-minute rounds, stop while it is still fun
